content: 1. If you are hospitalized, it is essential to consume a balanced diet that includes plenty of fruits and vegetables, lean protein, and whole grains to support overall health. 2. Dietary supplements, such as vitamins C and D or zinc, are not intended to treat or prevent COVID-19. However, these nutrients may influence immune system function, inflammation, and swelling. 3. The best way to obtain these nutrients is through food sources: vitamin C from fruits and vegetables, vitamin D from low-fat milk, fortified milk alternatives, and seafood, and zinc from lean meats, seafood, legumes, nuts, and seeds. 4. Patients can be discharged from the hospital when it is clinically appropriate. If discharged before the recommended isolation period ends, patients should continue isolation at home. 5. Decisions to discontinue transmission-based precautions or in-home isolation should be made on a case-by-case basis in consultation with clinicians, infection prevention specialists, and public health authorities. These decisions depend on factors such as disease severity, symptoms, and COVID-19 test results from respiratory specimens. 6. There is no evidence that coronaviruses, including SARS-CoV-2, can be transmitted through blood transfusion. Pre-donation screening procedures are in place to prevent donations from individuals with respiratory illness symptoms. 7. The CDC recommends placing visual alerts, such as signs and posters, at entrances and strategic locations to promote hand hygiene, respiratory hygiene (including the use of cloth face coverings), and cough etiquette. 8. Physical distancing should be maintained as much as possible. This includes using video conferencing, increasing workstation spacing, and reducing the number of individuals in common areas like breakrooms and elevators. 9. Visitors to inpatient facilities should be limited to those essential for the patient’s physical or emotional well-being. Visitors should be screened for fever and COVID-19 symptoms before entry, wear face masks, practice frequent hand hygiene, and restrict their visit to designated areas. 10. Hospitals should report daily counts of patients with suspected or confirmed COVID-19, the availability of hospital beds and mechanical ventilators, healthcare personnel staffing, and supply status. The NHSN provides state health departments access to COVID-19 data for hospitals in their jurisdictions. 11. Wastewater workers handling untreated waste from hospitals with COVID-19 patients should follow standard practices, including basic hygiene precautions and wearing recommended personal protective equipment (PPE). This includes goggles, protective face masks or splash-proof face shields, liquid-repellent coveralls, waterproof gloves, and rubber boots. 12. Basic hygiene precautions include washing hands with soap and water immediately after handling human waste or sewage, avoiding touching the face, and keeping open sores or cuts covered with clean, dry bandages. Workers should also remove soiled work clothes before eating and avoid smoking or chewing gum while handling waste. 13. For environmental services (EVS) personnel cleaning and disinfecting rooms of hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients, only essential personnel should enter these rooms. 14. Healthcare facilities may assign daily cleaning of high-touch surfaces to nursing personnel already providing care to the patient. If EVS personnel are responsible, they must wear all recommended PPE while in the room. PPE should be removed upon exiting the room, followed immediately by hand hygiene.
